name: Mike McDaniel

views.text: A player's health comes before any game, and the protocol is not something a coach gets to bend.
Telling players about your own failures earns more trust than pretending you never had any.
Results belong to the whole team, so no quarterback should carry a loss alone.
Outside criticism is mostly knee-jerk; dwelling on it only steals focus from the next game.
Being yourself in front of the room is a form of respect, not a lack of seriousness.
Football is won inside out; the line of scrimmage comes before any clever design.
The offense should be efficient enough that a star quarterback only has to be special when it truly counts.
Losing a job is humbling, and the useful answer is to get sharper at the next one.

signatures: answers a dry question with an offbeat joke, then gives a careful football answer
tells a story from his own rough years when a player is going through something
turns questions about a quarterback's mistakes toward the whole unit's execution
want: to unlock Justin Herbert's playoff ceiling as a play-caller and earn a second head-coaching job
fear: that the slide of his last two Miami offenses gets read as a scheme figured out rather than a quarterback hurt
voice: Quick, playful and openly unguarded; he jokes with reporters and wanders into long, thoughtful answers. Since his firing he sounds humbled but not bitter, talking about adapting to his players and adding value to people. When a player is hurt he turns serious and speaks about the person first, and he explains scheme in plain language.

evidence.summary: Camp feature: he shares his past struggles with alcohol and depression with players a little at a time, tells Tagovailoa about his own lowest moment as an assistant and stresses that results are collective. Players say it builds trust; his Yale coach praises how clearly he explains complex concepts.

Facing criticism of the team's handling of Tagovailoa, he says outside opinion is beyond his control and often knee-jerk, and that dwelling on it would pull his focus from the team. Shows how he talks about criticism, not whether it bothers him privately.

evidence.publisher: Associated Press (Tim Reynolds), via NBC 6 South Florida
evidence.summary: AP feature: he believes leaders owe people their genuine selves, is known for quick jokes in pressers and on the sideline, speaks openly about his past adversity, and players call him smart, relatable and passionate about their welfare. Profile with player quotes; favorable framing.

evidence.publisher: NBC Sports Bay Area, Angelina Martin
evidence.summary: Before facing San Francisco he credits Kyle Shanahan with seeing his potential early and giving him room to grow, jokes about their long friendship, and says his focus is on his own team and its winning streak. His own account of the relationship.

Miami fires him after a 7-10 season, its second straight losing year, with owner Stephen Ross citing a need for comprehensive change; he finishes 35-33 with playoff trips in his first two seasons, days after saying he was coach until told otherwise. Wire report.

The Chargers hire him as coordinator after Harbaugh fires Greg Roman; he had talked with several teams about head jobs; described as one of the top offensive minds from Shanahan's tree, expected to build a more versatile offense with simpler reads for Justin Herbert. Wire report.

evidence.publisher: Sports Illustrated (Dolphins on SI), Alain Poupart
evidence.summary: Introductory Chargers press conference: ties Miami's decline to Tagovailoa's injuries, calls the drop humbling, says scheme should fit the best players and that speed alone was not the answer, wants to add value to people daily, and still hopes to be a head coach again while focusing on this job.

Named the most important newcomer: he calls the plays, says he spent much of his career running the run game, frames football as inside out with the line of scrimmage first, and wants Herbert at his strongest in December and January. Team site citing The Athletic.
